title: Best garden tools for beginners
summary: The only tools you really need for your first garden
fullContent:
BEST GARDEN TOOLS FOR BEGINNERS: MUST-HAVE LIST

There's always a lot of hype surrounding new, cool garden tools, especially when influencers use them to grab your attention. The truth is, you probably don't need them! It can be tempting to hit 'add to cart', but we're here to tell you about the core tools we constantly reach for to complete garden tasks.

[IMG:data/images/ext-link-002-hero.jpg]

5 HAND TOOLS YOU'LL USE AGAIN AND AGAIN
1.
A TROWEL: Use it when transplanting, moving plants, or digging up deep-rooted weeds. An ergonomic design will alleviate wrist and hand pain.
2.
HAND FORK: Break up the soil in the spring, reduce small weeds, and pull strong roots from beneath the soil.
3.
PRUNERS: Every gardener has their favorite pair of hand pruners. Use them to harvest, deadhead, prune, and do general cleanup.
4.
WEEDERS: Uproot, cut, and scrape out the roots of unwanted plants. Dandelions don't stand a chance!
5.
HARVEST KNIFE: Popular for harvesting greens and herbs. Hori Hori knives are sharp and multi-purpose.

[IMG:data/images/ext-link-002-1.jpg]

BIGGER TOOLS FOR DIGGING AND SHAPING
Once your garden grows beyond a few raised beds, having a couple of sturdy digging tools will make soil prep and shaping beds much faster and easier.

Shovels and spades serve different purposes. A shovel has a longer handle and curved blade for moving compost, while a spade is shorter with a straight blade for cutting and edging.

[IMG:data/images/ext-link-002-2.jpg]

STORAGE AND MAINTENANCE
Performing some quick, general maintenance after each use will help keep your tools in top shape. Clear them of debris with a dry brush, dry them off, and optionally apply oil to the spring mechanism.

Use vertical space to store your tools. Add hooks and tool racks to small garden sheds. This keeps your tools accessible and safe from rust.

title: Light Deprivation: Greenhouse Science Explained
summary: Learn how to manipulate light cycles to trick your plants into flowering early.
fullContent:
LIGHT DEPRIVATION: HOW TO IMPLEMENT IT AND WHY YOU SHOULD

What is Light Deprivation?

Light deprivation is a useful growing technique often implemented to encourage or discourage flowering in plants outside their regular seasonal schedule. Using blackout tarps to simulate the seasons' changing, growers can take advantage of up to three harvests: early summer, late summer, and winter.

[IMG:data/images/ext-link-003-hero.jpg]

How do plants know when it's time to flower?

Plants collect information from their environment, actually right from their leaves. They are sensitive to light, temperature, and length of daylight (the photoperiod). Plants are categorized by how they react to changes in the photoperiod: Short-Day plants, Long-Day plants, and Day-Neutral.

1.
SHORT-DAY PLANTS: Require long nights to flower. They like to release their flowers or fruit in the fall. Examples: Chrysanthemum, Rice, Hemp, Soybeans, Hops, Onion, Violet.
2.
LONG-DAY PLANTS: Require short nights to flower. They need more than twelve hours of light a day. Examples: Aster, Hibiscus, Coneflower, Lettuce, Spinach, Radish, Sugar beets, Potato, Carrots.
3.
DAY-NEUTRAL PLANTS: Not affected by the number of night or day hours. They depend more on environmental conditions. Examples: Cucumbers, Tomatoes, Corn, Peas.

[IMG:data/images/ext-link-003-1.jpg]

Maximizing Your Harvest

Light Dep techniques can accelerate flowering in short-day plants. An excellent example is hops. These techniques enable the grower to harvest as early as July, three months before its natural harvest time. Not only would you have the product in the offseason, but there would also be an opportunity for a second harvest in the fall.

LIGHT DEP: HOW TO:
•
Start seedlings indoors under a grow light.
•
Use a light deprivation tarp to shield plants for 12 hours.
•
This schedule mimics the Fall Equinox.
•
Your plants will switch into flowering mode because they think it's much later in the season.

[IMG:data/images/ext-link-003-2.jpg]

Cons and Risks

These techniques, when properly executed, can mean extra profits. However, they can also lead to total loss if not managed correctly. Inconsistencies with coverage can shock your plants and leave them vulnerable to pests and diseases. For this reason, many rely on automated systems and timers in large greenhouse settings.
